title: Nanak's answer to the yogis
hookLine: the yogis ask Nanak his name, his path, where he comes from and where he goes
carry: my seat is the one in every heart

cards: Name. Place of residence. Purpose of visit.
Final destination. A passport desk wants four answers, and it wants them short. The yogis in the Sidh Gosht ask a stranger almost the same list.
Who are you? What's your name? What path are you on, and what are you after?
Where do you sit, where do you stay, where did you come from, and where are you going? They ask him, in paraphrase, to answer truthfully. Fair questions, for a guest.

teach.h: NO VILLAGE, NO CASTE, NO LINEAGE.
teach.b: Listen to what Nanak leaves out. No village, no family name, no caste, no sect, no teacher's lineage. His answer, in paraphrase: the One lives deep in every heart, and that is where I sit and where I stay.
I walk in the will of the True Guru. I came in the ease of the divine order, and I go wherever that order sends me. Nanak lives forever under that will.
My seat is the One who does not move; that's what the Guru's teaching gave me. And the one who turns toward the Guru comes to understand, recognizes their own self, and merges into the True.

teach.h: MY SEAT IS IN EVERY HEART.
teach.b: They asked where he sits, and he names a seat inside every heart.

teach.h: I GO WHERE THE ORDER SENDS ME.
teach.b: They asked where he comes from and where he's going, and instead of a road he gives a direction: the hukam, the order that sends him. They asked his path, and he says, more or less, I walk where I'm told.
That isn't dodging. It's answering one level down. A name tells you what to call someone; a hometown, where they started.
Nanak's answer tells you what he's oriented toward, the one thing a name never says. And near the end, a quiet phrase: aap pachhaanai, a person recognizes their own self.
In this poem, knowing who you are isn't something you hand over at the desk.
It's reached, by turning toward the Guru. The yogis' question was the right one. It's just bigger than they thought.

how: In katha on the Sidh Gosht, teachers often linger on this exchange, and Sikhs hear in Guru Nanak's answer the idea of living under hukam, the divine order, rather than defining oneself by caste or lineage.

o: a password the yogis asked of every guest at their circle
the yogis' first question, answered with a seat in every heart
a test of how long Nanak could hold a yogic pose

games.q: question and answer — tap the pairs.
p: the One lives in every heart

s: Nanak answers the yogis with his village and family name
he names no village, caste or lineage; he answers with a seat in every heart and the divine order.
the yogis ask where he comes from and where he is going
they ask who he is, his name, his path, his aim, where he came from and where he goes.
in the answer, knowing yourself comes by turning toward the Guru
the one who turns toward the Guru understands and recognizes their own self.

games.q: a circle of yogis asks you, a stranger: who are you, and where are you going? what does Nanak answer?
o: his name, his town and his family.
that he goes where the divine order sends him.
games.why: he answers one level down: the One lives in every heart, that's his seat, and he goes wherever the order sends him.

practice: Let the usual answers to who you are come up and pass by, your name, your job, your town, your role at home; they're all true, so set them down gently for a moment.
Then ask again underneath them, the way Nanak answered, by what you're turned toward, and when a line comes, even a clumsy one, hold it for a few breaths.
If you pray, set your line down under the hukam, the order Nanak said he walks in.

wordCard.voice: Who are you. The yogis' first question to Nanak, answered not with a name or a town but with a seat in every heart and a life lived under the divine order. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: my seat is the One in every heart. Nanak's answer isn't on a passport. Rest well.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ramkali, Mahala 1, Sidh Gosht, pauri 3, Ang 938 (the yogis' questions and Nanak's answer)
